AS.271.506.description: Research in environmental studies conducted under the direction of a faculty advisor.

prereqs.text: You must request Customized Academic Learning using the Customized Academic Learning form found in Student Self-Service: Registration > Online Forms.

AS.271.507.description: This course requires students to synthesize, integrate, and apply environmental skills and theory in a practical setting.

prereqs.text: You must request Customized Academic Learning using the Customized Academic Learning form found in Student Self-Service: Registration > Online Forms.

AS.271.509.description: This course is designed to accompany a supervised, hands-on experience working on an environmental or sustainability-related internship. In addition to completing 80 hours of applied work, students will prepare a reflective journal, paper, and poster presentation about their experience.

prereqs.text: You must request Customized Academic Learning using the Customized Academic Learning form found in Student Self-Service: Registration > Online Forms.

AS.271.511.description: Senior thesis research project in environmental science or environmental studies conducted under the direction of a faculty advisor.

prereqs.text: You must request Customized Academic Learning using the Customized Academic Learning form found in Student Self-Service: Registration > Online Forms.

AS.280.101.description: This course provides an overview of the field of public health. Topics include the major causes of morbidity and mortality; the socioeconomic, behavioral, and environmental factors that affect health; the analytical methods used in the field; the role of government in protecting the public’s health; key features of the U.S. health care system; and current challenges in the field. The course also introduces students to the basic conceptual models and approaches that are central to public health practice. This course is restricted to Sophomores who are declared Public Health Studies majors, and Freshman only.

AS.280.161.description: This course explores the intersection of biodiversity and public health. A combination of readings, documentaries, case studies, classroom discussions and in-class projects will be used to deepen our understanding of the role that the natural world plays in our emotional, social, physical and mental well-being. This course was designed for public health students who are not intending to pursue a career in natural sciences or medicine. This course satisfies the Public Health Studies Biology requirement but does not satisfy Pre-Med requirements. All first-year students must have taken or be currently enrolled in AS.280.101 to register. Instructor Approval Required.

AS.280.225.description: This course will cover the major world population changes in the past century as well as the contemporary situation and projections for this century. Topics include rapid population growth, the historical and continuing decline of death and birth rates, contraceptive methods as well as family planning and child survival programs, population aging, migration (including urbanization), population and the environment and a debate about whether the average person in the world in 2050 will be better or worse off than the average person today.

AS.280.240.description: This course examines the research process, with an emphasis on formulating research questions, critically evaluating published research, and drawing objective conclusions from a body of scientific literature. Students conduct a systematic review of the scientific literature related to a public health issue. Labs focus on developing and documenting a sound review methodology and communicating the review findings effectively in writing.

AS.280.331.description: The goal of this course is to prepare students to undertake the intersession study trip Global Health: Perspectives from Costa Rica. The course will introduce the socio-historical context of Costa Rica and provide an opportunity for group discussion before traveling together. We will apply a “global/local” framework to illustrate current health-related issues in the United States, to make comparisons when in Costa Rica. We will discuss the importance of cultural humility and positionality. Students will write reflections on course materials and participate in classroom discussion. Seats in this course will be limited to those who are accepted to the Costa Rica Intersession course, as determined by the Public Health Studies Program.

AS.280.333.description: This course introduces students to the role of policy, politics, and advocacy in public health. Students will learn how policy can function as a tool for intervention and how advocacy campaigns are developed and implemented. Using a project-based format, students will identify a public health issue of interest and develop an advocacy plan over the course of the semester. The final plan will include a policy goal, stakeholder analysis, communication materials, and an implementation and evaluation strategy. This seminar is a component of the Hopkins DC Semester themed Public Health: Evidence to Action.
restrictions: Hopkins Semester in DC Students Only

AS.280.334.description: The Hopkins Semester DC Applied Practitioner Seminar (Public Health Studies: Evidence to Action) is a core course for the Hopkins Semester. The course provides students critical access to political, policy, and media institutions, while also placing students within the actual communities that they are observing and analyzing. This practitioner course will draw in key actors from a variety of institutions: staffers and officials from federal and state government, lobbyists, journalists and media personalities, corporations, think tanks, and more. Students will engage with questions relating to public health, advocacy, and public health themes in dialog with practitioners and scholars who work in and around the field daily.
restrictions: Hopkins Semester in DC Students Only

AS.280.335.description: This course surveys the basic concepts underlying environmental health sciences (toxicology, exposure assessment, risk assessment), current public health issues (air, water- and food-borne diseases) and global health threats (climate change, designing healthy communities, and environmental justice).

AS.280.340.description:
Through lectures and small group discussions, students will develop a framework for analyzing health care policy problems and gain familiarity with current issues including managed care, Medicare and the uninsured.
Public Health Studies majors have 1st priority for enrollment. Your enrollment may be withdrawn at the discretion of the PHS program if you are not a PHS major.

AS.280.341.description: Developing intersectional approaches for health interventions requires the inclusion of all people, including men. This course will examine men’s health through different psychological perspectives: biological, social learning, social constructionist, feminist, and intersectional. Students will be asked to critique and experience approaches used to address men’s health issues, programmatic activities, and measure change of men’s health outcomes. Coursework requires the review and application of global men’s health theories, frameworks, and policies. The interplay of masculinity and health will be explored throughout the course by diving into research and experiencing programmatic interventions for health topics such as: family planning, mental health and loneliness, and care work.

AS.280.345.description: Using problem-based learning focusing on public health topics, students learn to describe & summarize data, make inferences regarding population parameters, & test hypotheses. Recommended Course Background: Four years of high school math.

AS.280.346.description: Formerly known as Advanced Biostatistics Laboratory, a complementary course to 280.345, Public Health Biostatistics, this course teaches R programming skills necessary for conducting independent data analyses, beyond those presented in the main course. No programming experience is necessary, but a willingness to learn independently and work with other students is indispensable.

AS.280.347.description: Students will learn to formulate precise scientific and policy questions, design exploratory and confirmatory statistical analyses to address the questions, conduct appropriate analyses using the statistical package R, and communicate their findings through graphical and tabular displays that are presented in writing and in person. The course will be run seminar style in which students conduct data analysis to present to one another in one meeting per week. Evaluation will be through class participation and a final project in which students will analyze their own data set to address a question of their choice. Students need to have taken an introductory statistics course at the level of AS.280.345 (Public Health Biostatistics) and must have some experience using the statistical software R to perform basic analyses.

AS.280.350.description: A practical introduction to epidemiology focusing on the principles and methods of examining the distribution and determinants of disease morbidity and mortality in human populations.

AS.280.355.description: Introduces students to a social ecological perspective of population health; Explains key theories and models of health behavior; Describes social and behavioral factors affecting health outcomes; Illustrates the role of factors such as racism, income inequality, social norms, culture, communication and psychological constructs in health outcomes; Demonstrates applications of these theories and models in health behavior research and intervention.

AS.280.365.description: This course is composed of lectures on issues that impact the arena of public health and public policy, viewed through a health equity lens. With real-life examples of public health and public policy issues and practices in Baltimore and around the country, this course will provide real-life experiences in the fields of public health and public policy. Throughout the course a major effort will also be made to expose students to the wide array of opportunities that are available to those pursuing a career in public health.

prereqs.text: Antirequisite: Students who have already completed, or are currently enrolled in as.280.366, are not eligible to enroll in AS.280.365.

AS.280.366.description: This course will examine the role of politics in Public Health. It will cover the legislative process at the local, state and federal level, as well as the role of the executive branch/administrative agencies in implementing new policies. The course will also discuss ways that those involved in the public health arena can influence legislation, policy and budgets as part of the political process.

AS.280.380.description: Global health addresses the staggering global disparities in health status, drawing on epidemiology, demography, anthropology, economics, international relations and other disciplines. We review patterns of mortality, morbidity and disability in low and middle income countries, starting with malnutrition, infectious diseases and reproductive health, and continuing to an emerging agenda including mental health, injury prevention, surgical care, chronic diseases, and health impacts of climate change. Gender, health systems and health workforce challenges, and career trajectories in global health are also discussed. Recommended course background: Minimum of one prior course in Public Health.

AS.280.389.description: The goal of this course is to introduce students to the importance and value of partnerships between medical/health institutions and community organizations to improve community and neighborhood health outcomes. This course will discuss how community engagement can assist in population health concerns and challenges faced in clinical settings through the promotion of community health. Discussed through the viewpoints of a health system and clinician, the how and why of community engagement will be explored, centering on how to create a medical-community relationship, executing engagements and projects, and measuring vital outcomes to reaffirm these partnerships’ significance. This course will combine lectures, class discussions, and services learning. Students, in teams, will complete 40 hours of service learning outside of class time for a community-based organization. This course qualifies as a PHS Upper Level Elective. Students cannot register for this course and AS.280.379.

prereqs.text: Students who took or are taking AS.280.379 are not permitted to take AS.280.389.
AS.280.101 must be completed prior to registering for AS.280.389.

AS.280.390.description: In this course, students will learn how to build effective public health partnerships with communities. We will discuss history, contexts, and structures of power that influence communities’ social determinants of health. We will also explore sociological, educational, and organizational theories and methods that center community voices and build partnerships that improve community health. This course is valuable to students who want to prepare themselves for working with communities using anti-oppressive practices. By the course’s conclusion, students should understand how to account for and address the systems, history, and positions of power that affect the success of community projects related to social determinants of health.

AS.280.399.description: This course introduces students to a social structural, justice orientation to public health, with an emphasis on service learning in Baltimore City. Through lectures, class discussions, reflection practices and experiential learning, students will gain an understanding of education, healthcare, housing and other sectors as social determinants of health. The course draws on a social ecological framework and highlights the role of relationships and policies in impacting community resources foundational to health and well-being. Students will choose a community-based organization according to their interests and schedule and, working in teams, complete 45 hours of service-based learning. Grades are based on class participation, completion of a service learning project, group presentation, and papers. Open to Junior Public Health Studies majors and, space permitting, to others upon permission of instructor. This course qualifies as a PHS upper elective; however, it does not satisfy the PHS Applied Experience requirement.

AS.280.485.description: Food as Medicine explores how diet influences disease progression and health outcomes through the lens of the gut microbiome. Coursework will emphasize the immunological and physiological mechanisms underlying diet-mediated effects on human health including how factors like affordability, access to foods adhering to public health standards of high-quality nutrition, education, and continuous access to medical care and nutrition support programs can modulate the benefits of health-promoting diets on a population scale. This course emphasizes active, collaborative learning through primary literature, presentations and real-world problem-solving. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.486.description: Epidemiology is the study of the causes and distributions of disease, injury, illness, disability, and death in human populations so that we can identify ways to intervene, preventing disease and promoting health. Legal epidemiology and public health law research focus on policies as factors in the cause, distribution, and prevention of health outcomes in a population. This course will introduce students to the field of legal epidemiology and the methods used to examine how laws and policies exert effects on population health. Using the dual criminalization of homelessness and substance use as an illustrative case study, students will gain skills and hands-on experience using scientific legal mapping and qualitative research methods to better understand shifts in this policy landscape and its public health implications. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.487.description: Menstrual pain. Endometriosis. Uterine fibroids. Pelvic inflammatory disease. Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Why are reproductive-health symptoms so often normalized, misunderstood, or dismissed? How do stigma, gender norms, racial inequities, and health systems shape what is considered “normal,” when people seek care, and whether they receive an accurate diagnosis and effective treatment? This discussion-based seminar examines how reproductive-health symptoms are experienced, normalized, diagnosed, and treated. Through research articles, patient narratives, case studies, and interactive activities, students will examine how historical beliefs, social relationships, stigma, and health-system barriers influence reproductive-health experiences across diverse social and geographic settings. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically evaluate care-seeking pathways, identify barriers at multiple levels, and propose and develop evidence-informed public-health solutions. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.488.description: This course examines how structural determinants of health — the policies, systems, and power arrangements that shape neighborhood disadvantage — drive mental health and brain development across the life course. Using a place-based approach grounded in structural violence and life-course theory, students will apply geospatial analysis to map the conditions and population patterns underlying these health inequities and connect this understanding to neuroscience research on how chronic stress and environmental exposures shape developing brains and mental health outcomes. Throughout, students will critically examine how these differences are rooted in structural and environmental conditions rather than deficits within individuals, families, or cultural groups, and how research on them is interpreted, communicated, and used in policy and practice. A Biology background would be helpful in this course. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.489.description: Climate change and interlinked threats like antimicrobial resistance are already reshaping infectious disease risk — and the global health infrastructure built to detect and respond to that risk is under constraint in real time. Disease surveillance helps answer critical questions: what is happening, where, and among whom? Signaling public health officials to investigate why – and what should be done about it? This seminar uses a recurring framework — does surveillance exist for this threat? What can it tell us, given how it was built? Who acts on that information, and how? — to examine a different climate-sensitive infectious disease or related health system challenge each week. Students will learn the infrastructure disease surveillance requires; how surveillance data is used to justify funding and drive policy and intervention decisions; what research questions remain open in this space; and what career paths exist for people who want to work at the intersection of epidemiology, data, and action. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically evaluate a real surveillance system, trace how (or whether) data translates into policy and funding decisions, and design a surveillance or response strategy under realistic, resource-constrained conditions. The course focuses on surveillance as the connective tissue between epidemiologic data and health system action — using the current restructuring of U.S. global health operations as a live, unfolding case. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.490.description: This course examines what it takes for youth participation in global health to be real rather than symbolic. Young people are increasingly involved in designing and delivering health programs, from HIV prevention and treatment to adolescent mental health services. Their participation is built on the premise that their involvement makes programs more relevant and more likely to reach those they are meant to serve. Yet when a program reports that it engaged youth, what that meant in practice is rarely specified, and involvement and authority are not the same thing, presenting an Illusion of Inclusion. In this seminar, we will explore the models and typologies that describe youth participation, the contextual factors such as funding, policy, and cultural norms that shape what engagement is possible, and the mechanisms through which participation falls short of its promise, including tokenism, co-optation, adultism, and epistemic injustice. Central to the course is an examination of power and how it operates within global health participation structures. Through a combination of lectures, global case studies, class discussions with guest speakers who lead this work in their own countries, and a simulation game in which student teams build a participation structure and then assess the choices they made, students will analyze real-world examples of youth engagement and learn to distinguish meaningful participation from inclusion that is only symbolic. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to evaluate how youth are engaged in health programs, identify where authority actually sits, and propose ways of structuring decisions that give young people genuine, shared ownership. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.491.description: In this course we will examine the three central tenets of reproductive justice: the right to have children, the right not to have children, and the right to parent one’s children in safe and healthy environments. We will apply this framework to a variety of critical sexual and reproductive health topics including contraception, abortion, adoption, procreative technologies, and surrogacy. We will also center conversations of equity and identity by interrogating how sex, gender, race, income, sexuality, and disability impact a person’s access to reproductive liberty. This course will draw from a range of disciplines including ethics and philosophy, law and policy, and public health research. Course materials will also include a range of media including books, research articles, podcasts, and film. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.492.description: Chronic pain is a major public health crisis that affects more than 20% of U.S. adults. This interdisciplinary course examines how pain is experienced, measured, and studied through the perspectives of biology, statistics, public health, and the humanities. Students will learn about a wide range of pain assessment tools, examine how scientific evidence is generated and interpreted, and discuss contemporary issues such as the opioid crisis and disparities in pain experience through real-world case studies. Ultimately, the course invites students to draw these perspectives together for a fuller understanding of pain, one that goes beyond what any single lens can offer on its own. This is a Gordis Teaching Fellowship course. Priority registration is given to Public Health Studies majors. Other students will be permitted to register as space allows.

AS.280.495.description: Using lectures, oral presentations, and writing assignments, this seminar is designed to assist Public Health Studies majors in writing a senior thesis. Students will formulate their topics, develop research skills, and address issues of professional ethics. Participating in this seminar is required for students pursuing honors in Public Health Studies. Permission Required.

AS.280.499.description: A research methods seminar to prepare students doing honors in Public Health Studies. Permission Required.

AS.280.500.description: Perm. Req'd, Public Health Majors Only. This is a supervised, hands-on experience working with public health professionals. Students will complete 80 hours of applied work and will submit a synthesizing assignment at the end of the term. Students completing their AE in the current semester will be enrolled in Section 2. Students whose time will roll over to an additional grading period will be enrolled in Section 1. Please contact your PHS Advisor for complete details.

AS.290.101.description: This course examines the origins of human structure, function and behavior from an evolutionary perspective. It includes study of the evolution, behavior and behavioral ecology of nonhuman primates, hominid evolution (including the paleontological and archaeological records), and the origins of human cognition, social behavior and culture.

AS.290.303.description: In this course, students DO science through experiments in animal behavior and animal communication. Students will learn how to design experiments, analyze results and write scientific papers in publication form. Students will work on one class experiment for their first paper and then design and conduct their own experiment for their second paper. The course is held in the Undergraduate Teaching Laboratory on campus.

AS.290.306.description: This course examines the evolution of behavior via natural and sexual selection through the study of model organisms (e.g., fish, insects) in the laboratory and the field. Students will learn how to design and run experiments, analyze results, and write scientific papers in publication form. Students will work on multiple research projects throughout the semester. The course is held in the Undergraduate Teaching Laboratory on campus. Behavioral Biology majors only; all other majors will need to seek approval from the instructor.

AS.290.307.description: The course examines human behavior from an evolutionary perspective. Lectures and seminar-based discussion of the primary literature will cover some of the major approaches and areas of study within the fields of (1) evolutionary anthropology, (2) evolutionary psychology, (3) human behavioral ecology, and (4) evolutionary medicine.

AS.290.330.description: Course focuses on sexual development, sexuality across the lifespan, gender identity, sexual attraction and arousal, sexually transmitted disease, and the history of commercial sex workers and pornography. Please note that the use of electronic devices is not permitted during this class, in order to promote the full interactive potential of this engaging seminar-style offering. Open to Juniors & Seniors within the following majors/minors: Behavioral Biology; Biology; Cognitive Science; Medicine, Science & the Humanities; Molecular & Cellular Bio; Neuroscience; Psychological & Brain Sciences; Public Health; Sociology; Study of Women, Gender, & Sexuality.

AS.290.450.description: Qualified students can serve as undergraduate Teaching Assistants for behavioral biology courses they have already taken at Hopkins (by faculty instructor invitation only). Each individual faculty instructor will determine TA responsibilities based upon departmental policy. Upon invitation, potential Teaching Assistants should forward the instructor invitation to the Director of Undergraduate Studies (Dr. Bohn) and make a request in SIS to add the course using the instructor’s section number.

AS.290.490.description: Great ideas in Behavioral Biology. Discussion of classic and cutting edge articles in the original literature. Student presentations and reaction papers. Capstone course for senior Behavioral Biology majors.

prereqs.text: AS.200.141 AND AS.200.208 AND AS.290.101 or instructor permission.

AS.290.495.description: In this seminar, students discuss the intellectual merit of current or potential future research, internship and outreach activities in Behavioral Biology. This course is designed to 1) expose Behavioral Biology majors to new knowledge in the field, 2) provide the opportunity to develop oral and written communication skills, and 3) build community among students in the major. Students will make oral presentations and write a short paper/news piece or prepare a webpage. This class will meet twice during the semester. The first meeting will run until 6 p.m. and the second meeting until ~8 p.m. The two meeting dates will be announced at the beginning of the spring semester.

AS.290.501.description: Students will receive a hands-on experience conducting Behavioral Biology Research with the faculty member listed on this section who must approve your enrollment. In addition to participating in laboratory research students are required to submit a research style paper summarizing their work that is approved by their mentor. Information on the paper, research credits and how to enroll can be found at https://krieger.jhu.edu/behavioralbiology/research/ . Students working in Dr. Moss’s lab must also register for AS.290.400 Comparative Neural Systems and Behavior Research Discussions.

Pre-approval by the DUS of Behavioral Biology is required. In addition to participating in laboratory research students are required to submit a research style paper summarizing their work that is approved by their mentor and submitted to the DUS. AS.290.519.description: An independent study is when you pursue a topic of special interest within Behavioral Biology. You must initiate the process. The independent study project must be pre-approved by the DUS of Behavioral Biology and must culminate in a substantial research or topic paper submitted to the DUS. For more information visit https://krieger.jhu.edu/behavioralbiology/research/.

Students are required to submit a paper summarizing their internship experience that is a approved by their internship mentor and submitted to the DUS. For more information visit https://krieger.jhu.edu/behavioralbiology/research/.

AS.300.102.description: This course offers an introductory survey of foundational authors of modern philosophy and moral and political thought whose ideas continue to influence contemporary problems and debates. The course is taught in lectures and seminar discussions. Authors studied include Plato, René Descartes, Immanuel Kant, Karl Marx, Virginia Woolf, Ludwig Wittgenstein, Iris Murdoch, James Baldwin, Cora Diamond, Judith Butler, Kwame A. Appiah and others.

AS.300.202.description:
Socrates once declared, “the unexamined life is not worth living.” Every work in this course takes up the challenge of discovering what kind of life is worth living. From Montaigne, who made his own shifting self the subject of his Essays, to the searching plays and novels of Shakespeare, Cervantes, Flaubert, Woolf, and Coetzee and the daring arguments of Descartes, Kant, Nietzsche, and Beauvoir, these thinkers and writers ask what it means to know oneself and to find meaning in a world that offers no ready answers.
Taking our cue from Montaigne’s essai – an attempt or trial – we will practice inquiry by weighing ideas, testing them against experience, and thinking through them in writing and in dialogue with these texts and one another. Team-taught by faculty from Philosophy, Comparative Thought and Literature, and Modern Languages and Literatures, this course aims to bring together minds from different disciplines around questions that belong to everyone. All texts will be distributed to students at the beginning of the semester, and students will have the opportunity to take part in device-free Reading Parties throughout the term. We welcome students from all backgrounds who seek the kind of slow, sustained reading that these works afford and who are open to ideas that may change how they understand their own lives.

AS.300.215.description: This course will examine the relationship between law and literature. As many have observed, literature and law have much in common as well as much to teach each other. Topics this course will discuss include practices of interpretation, issues of authority, and the power of narrative. In addition to reading essays by scholars in the field, students will read a selection of judicial opinions, short stories, novels, and plays. Final grades will be based on class participation, three in-class essays, and a group project due at the end of the semester.

AS.300.309.description: This year marks the centenary of Martin Heidegger’s "Being and Time," arguably the most important work of philosophy in the 20th century. Often considered an impenetrable book, in this course we will aim at a clear and jargon-free understanding of the overarching stakes and shape of its argument, as well as its individual passages and steps. To that end, we will work our way through the text as closely and systematically as possible.

prereqs.text: Students who have already taken, or are currently enrolled in AS.300.616, are not eligible to take AS.300.309.

AS.300.311.description: Modernity has often been described as the age in which God has died. But concern with the nature and experience of divinity pervades modern literary texts. In this course we will sample a variety of works from the nineteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first centuries that investigate the possibilities and limitations of religious belief under the conditions of modernity. Authors to be read include Kierkegaard, G. M. Hopkins, George Eliot, Friedrich Nietzsche, Franz Kafka, Virginia Woolf, Hermann Hesse, C. S. Lewis, T. S. Eliot, W. H. Auden, Solvej Balle, and Jon Fosse. This class counts towards the requirements of a text-based course for the minor in Comparative Thought and Literature.

AS.300.315.description: What is the proper role of the arts and artists in society? Is censorship of the arts or artists ever permissible, for political or other reasons? How may artists and their publics challenge conventional frames of reference or control, state-sponsored or otherwise? Are any of the arts better suited than others to resistance or opposition? Are any of the arts better suited than the others to fostering control and compliance? This class will employ a comparative framework to examine these and other central questions raised by theories and histories of authoritarianism and the arts. It will investigate various theoretical and philosophical frameworks for understanding its key concepts, ranging from Plato, Kant, and Tolstoy to Dewey, Adorno, Arendt, and beyond. The class will concentrate on specific case studies drawn from across world history, beginning with examples from the early modern era, moving into the twentieth-century (including Nazi Germany, fascist Italy, the USSR, China, and the US 1950s, 1960s, and 1980s), and ending with the present day worldwide. It will draw on various art forms, including music, visual arts, literature, film, and various combinations of these and other art forms.

AS.300.319.description: When you are working for a business, how do you distinguish your ideas, actions, and responsibilities from the firms’—if that is even possible? What is corporate culture or a corporate person, and how is it similar or different from any other kind of culture or person? These and related questions inspired and fascinated writers from the nineteenth century through the present. By reading and thinking about short stories, novels, films, and a play, we will explore these issues and potential resolutions to them. The course especially considers how problems of action, agency, and responsibility in capitalism become an intriguing challenge for writers and filmmakers. Texts by Herman Melville, Willa Cather, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Alice Munro, and George Saunders, and David Mamet; films Charlie Chaplin, Boots Riley, Kitty Green, and Bong Joon-ho.

AS.300.320.description: Wars make history. But does history necessarily provide an adequate account of the human experiences caused by war? In this course, we examine how literature and film in modern East Asia transformed and reinvented themselves through their engagement with experiences of war, and explore what these forms of expression tell us about human existence when everyday life is stripped away. With a focus on literature and film produced in the contexts of conflicts during early nation-building in East Asia, the wars waged by imperial Japan, and the civil wars in China and Korea, we explore questions such as: How do literature and film take part in wartime propaganda? How do they remember wartime suffering, atrocities, and trauma? How do they reckon with memories of perpetration? How do they represent war as a gendered experience? How do they contribute to transitional justice? As we interrogate these questions, we also consider how their forms of expression changed in response to shifting social and political circumstances in the postwar periods. We will discuss literary and cinematic works originally produced in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean with reference to philosophical writings on concepts including “tragedy,” “memory,” “justice,” and “contingency.” All readings are in English, and all films are subtitled in English.

AS.300.327.description:
In this seminar in comparative world drama, students will study major works for theatre which use the stage not as a means of pleasure and instruction, as it had been understood for centuries, but as a means of revolutionizing the social order. By reconceiving the stage as political in nature, these theatre artists also ushered in a revolution of theatrical aesthetics.
The course will begin with and include a residency from Anna Deavere Smith, a former MacArthur Fellow and recipient of the National Humanities Medal from President Barack Obama, as she workshops her in-process play about the history of racism in Maryland and at Johns Hopkins University.
It will also encompass classical texts dealing with revolt against the political order as well as works from Russian, German, South American, and East and South Asian political theater artists.
Students will study dramatic texts, films, and theoretical works by formative figures such as Vladislav Meyerhold and Sergei Eisenstein, Bertolt Brecht and Walter Benjamin, Griselda Gambaro and Augusto Boal, Girish Karnad and Luis Valdez, among others. The course charts a trajectory from the Bolshevik radicalism of 1917 in eastern Europe to the colonial diaspora of the postwar era, ending in the seat of modern-day American imperialism, linking uprisings and social protest movements to an aesthetic language developed over space and time.

AS.300.372.description:
- You know, Hela, you’re an anxious human being. She:
- I’m a human being?
- Why, of course. You’re not a puppy.
She pondered. After a long pause, surprised:
- I’m a human being. I’m Hela. I’m a girl. I’m Polish. I’m mommy’s little daughter, I’m from Warsaw…. What a lot of things I am!
Janusz Korczak, Ghetto Diary
This course isn’t what you expect. We will tackle painful topics: orphanhood, loneliness, jealousy, death. You will learn that “Snow White expresses, more perfectly than any other fairy-tale, the idea of melancholy” (Adorno). We will also deal with parenthood, childhood, justice, and love. We will not watch any Disney films. Who is a child? “Children are not people of tomorrow; they are people today,” wrote in 1919 Janusz Korczak, pediatrician, and children’s author who believed in children’s rights. We will read folk tales, authorial fairy tales (Oscar Wilde), fantasy books (Tove Jansson’s Moomintrolls) and science-fiction (Stanisław Lem’s Fables for Robots). We will also investigate the special connection between children and animals (Juan Rámon Jimenez, Margaret Wise Brown). Many iconic children’s literature characters, such as Peter Pan, “a Betwixt-and-Between,” Little Prince, and Pippi Longstocking, are outsiders. All along we will consider how children’s literature reflects and shapes ideas of selfhood, from archetypal to post-humanistic ones.

AS.300.399.description: What do films and philosophy have in common? Do films express, with their own means, philosophical problems that are relevant to our experience of ourselves and the world we live in? This term we will study such issues with a particular focus on questions of justice, truth, revenge, forgiveness, hope, hate, and fear.

prereqs.text: Students who are enrolled in or have completed AS.300.699 are not eligible to take AS.300.399.

AS.300.441.description:
Readings from the works of Thoreau and Whitman, with an eye toward how they explore the multi-specied process of influence upon subjectivity-formation. “Influence” names the incursion, absorption, digestion, and transformation of an outside (including bodies, ideas, affects, elements, moods, atmospheres) into a subjectivity experienced as an inside. What are the powers and limits of Whitman’s and Thoreau’s experiments with language and writing (rhetoric, syntax, imagery, myth) as they seek to induce, inflect, combat, and transform influences? What role do their physical encounters with nonhuman agencies (of plants, animals, objects, divinities) play in, first, the way such encounters are turned into words (depicted and described) and, second, in the degree and kind of influence that those encounters and words have upon us as readers?
Cross listed with Political Science

AS.300.616.description: This year marks the centenary of Martin Heidegger’s Being and Time, arguably the most important work of philosophy in the 20th century. Often considered an impenetrable book, in this course we will aim at a clear and jargon-free understanding of the overarching stakes and shape of its argument, as well as its individual passages and steps. To that end, we will work our way through the text as closely and systematically as possible.

AS.300.621.description: When is an action or a work of art just an accident--and when should it be called intentional? This course explores the problems and complications of willed actions, accidents, and unintended consequences. We will follow (primarily but not exclusively) a range of different modernist writers, surrealist and dada artists, noir filmmakers, and twentieth-century philosophers as they contemplate what an intentional action is or is not. What can these works tell us about how we make meaning at the limits of our control? Includes literature of Wallace Stevens, Nathanael West, James Cain, Patricia Highsmith, and Ann Petry; films of Alfred Hitchcock, Billy Wilder, and Justine Triet; art of Marcel Duchamp and André Breton; and philosophy of Ludwig Wittgenstein, Elizabeth Anscombe, and Philippa Foot.

AS.300.627.description: In the wake of World War II and decolonization, French philosophers and intellectuals felt the need to reassess the legacy of European thought to understand its complicity in horrific forms of historical violence and engaged in a radical critique of the traditional philosophical concepts of identity, subjectivity, autonomy, agency, and rationality. Despite their differences, they shared the aim to produce a philosophical critique of philosophy itself and advance a different understanding of reason, individuality, power, responsibility and, more generally, of ethics and politics. Their ideas had, and continue to have, a widespread influence in contemporary debates at the global scale.This seminar will study such set of issues in the works of Simone de Beauvoir, Foucault, Deleuze, Lévinas, Derrida, Hélène Cixous, and others.

AS.300.633.description: Presentations by faculty, students, and invited speakers.

AS.300.802.description: Graduate student having directed work with a specific faculty.

AS.300.803.description: Dissertation research and discussion of progress. Limited to students writing dissertations.

AS.300.813.description: Teaching assistants are required to register for this course. See handbook for details.

AS.305.246.description: How do displaced people turn their experiences into stories? What can narratives of displacement teach us about the formation of individual and collective memory, the construction of personhood, and the placeness of diaspora, at once real and imagined? In this seminar, we examine the facts, fables, and fictions of displacement to and from the United States as constructed in literature, film, visual art, popular media, and personal accounts. Our investigations may include Chinese labor on the transcontinental railroad; Germans fleeing fascism in Los Angeles; Black Americans’ self-exile; forced displacement after Hurricane Katrina; Latin American immigration; and migration patterns in Silicon Valley. Working though these events, we will map differences and commonalities in modes of displacement and analyze the structure and quality of their narratives. Theoretical texts will orient and deepen our investigations; these may include works by Homi Bhabha, Richard Wright, Mike Davis, Cherríe Moraga, Fred Moten, Louise Pratt, Theodor Adorno. Student assignments will present opportunities for informal and formal writing and small group collaborations.

AS.305.288.description: This course surveys the stories and storytellers of moments of resistance and revolution. Possibilities include the 1967 Detroit rebellion, the Algerian War of Independence, Occupy, Arab Spring, Women Life Freedom, Peronism, Zapatistas, the Soweto Uprising, and interwar antifascist movements. We will critically examine how such moments are, or become, narratives, the form these narratives take, and how they acquire afterlives. To this end we will investigate a variety of materials, produced from a variety of points of view: the press, participants, observers, commentators, instigators, theorists, and those reconstructing the events after the fact as histories or fictions. Key themes include notions of personhood, citizenship, solidarity, empire, independence, the intersection of political thought and narrative, and the representation of social uprisings in a variety of media. Student assignments will provide opportunities for individual and collaborative engagement with course themes. Readings and viewings may include the works of Third Cinema, Joshua Oppenheimer, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, Peter Weiss, Manuel Puig, Silvia Federici, Naomi Klein, Corky Lee, Audre Lorde, Frantz Fanon, and Joshua Clover.

AS.305.336.description: The term “counterinsurgency” is typically associated with the disastrous US wars in Vietnam or Iraq. But is counterinsurgency always doomed to fail and insurgency guaranteed to succeed? This course will give students an overview of key literature in counterinsurgency and internal security, as well as representative literature produced by and for insurgents, revolutionaries, and guerrillas/terrorists. A central task will be to define these vexed terms and track their shifting meaning over time, including the importance of cultural, racial, and gendered significations to those definitions. The course will also include a large-scale simulation of an insurgency and efforts to control or extinguish it, comprising the student assignments and requiring active participation of every student in the course. Each student will be assigned roles that will require specific creative actions.

AS.305.350.description: This seminar offers students an opportunity to combine historical research skills and community engagement for real-world, public impact. Through collaborative research and partnering with an immigrant justice organization, students in the seminar will gain a deeper understanding of immigration history, gather and analyze research for community stakeholders, and transform scholarly discussions into applicable resources for use in immigrant rights and justice cases today. Students who wish to take this course should have previously enrolled in at least one course covering immigration, but that is not a formal prerequisite.

AS.305.510.description: Undergraduate independent research under a faculty mentor.

AS.310.202.description: From North Korea’s nuclear threat to South Korea’s K-pop, Korea is constantly in the US media. But how much do you know about Korea? This introductory course is designed to introduce students to the long and complex cultural history of Korea. While focusing on key aspects in shaping premodern and modern Korean identity, the course also places Korea in a larger cross-national context, particularly its close interactions with China and Japan. Reading primary and secondary sources combined with visual materials, the course chronologically and thematically examines major historical moments, from Korea’s participation in and exit from a Sino-centric premodern world order, Japanese colonialism and its ramifications in Korean society, economic development and democratization, to the global popularity of Korean popular culture.

AS.310.209.description: Coined by the late political scientist, Joseph Nye, “soft power,” — or the ability to influence others through attraction and persuasion rather than coercion —is often assumed to translate naturally into outcomes. This course tests that assumption, probing exactly how soft power shapes foreign policy in Asia. Students examine the dynamics of soft power and its history in the region; the media narratives and public opinion through which attraction is perceived and the resulting foreign policy behavior of countries in the region, including how small and middle powers use soft power as a tool for hedging between great-power rivals. The course also examines soft power from outside the region — including religious and cultural diplomacy in states with significant Muslim populations. Through the theoretical literature, case studies, group-led case presentations and guest speakers, the course interrogates the conditions under which soft power may “work” — and the instances in which it demonstrably fails to have an impact on policy. Introductory coursework in international relations or East Asian history recommended but not required.

AS.310.216.description: Urban China has gone through two major social transformations since 1949: the embrace of a central planning socialist system between early 1950s and late 70s, and the embrace of neo-liberal market economy in the so-call “socialism with Chinese characteristics” since 1980. While the political regime remains the same over time, many profound changes have occurred in economic life, social life, cultural life, spiritual life, and civil life. What really happened in the social transformation of urban China? What would explain those changes? How did people in different walk of life deal with those huge and deep social transformation? To address these concerns, we will exam a list of issues. Topics includes changes in population and demographic characteristics, employment structure and job market, workplace and residential communities, income and wealth distributions, segregation impacts of urban household registration systems, urban consumption patterns, courting cultures and dressing codes, spiritual practices, and social mobility and social stratifications. In the realm of public policies, we will pay special attentions to the issues of transportation, housing, medical service, public education, social insurance, and environmental protection. We will also study the characteristics of contentious politics and how social conflicts of power, interest, justice, cultural and belief were processed in urban China.

AS.310.305.description: The global political and security landscape of the 21st century will be shaped by the rivalry between two superpowers -- China and the U.S. For the foreseeable future, the geographic focus of that contest will be Southeast Asia and the surrounding maritime space, particularly the South China Sea. Southeast Asia is a complex, highly differentiated region of ten-plus nations, each with its own unique history and relationship with China. This course will introduce Southeast Asia as a key region -- geographically, economically, and strategically -- often overlooked by policymakers and scholars. It will also focus on the craft of national security strategy as the best tool for understanding the multi-sided competition, already well underway involving China, the U.S., and the Southeast Asian states.

AS.310.329.description: We will try to get a quick overview of the recent history of patriarchy in China, South Korea, and Japan from the mid-twentieth century to our present and then compare the initiatives of feminists to transform the lives of women throughout these three societies. We will also debate whether or how it makes sense to adapt the Western notions of patriarchy and sexism as well as the Western political program of feminism to the non-Western context of East Asia by reading books by historians, anthropologists, and sociologists.

AS.310.331.description: You will learn about the efforts of ordinary, non-elite Muslims to shape the relation between their communities and the state as well as to (where applicable) the non-Muslim majority through collective organizing over the last forty years. We will read and discuss books by anthropologists, historians, and sociologists studying Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, China, Malaysia, and Indonesia.

AS.310.332.description: Ever since the Chinese Empire fell in 1911, Chinese have tried to think of themselves as modern and to build a modern Chinese state. Among the Western concepts that Chinese appropriated to define and comprehend themselves were the notions of ethnicity, culture, nationality, and race. We will try to answer the following questions: What was the allure of arcane and elusive Western categories on culture, ethnicity, and race for Chinese scientists in the 20th century, and how did these categories come to underpin the rule of the Chinese state over its enormous population since the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949? How have the Chinese state’s policies on nationality and ethnicity shaped the minds of American China scholars as they study ethnicity and nationality in China?

AS.310.336.description: On 13 October 2022, a middle-aged upper-middle class Chinese man staged a public political protest on an elevated road in Beijing. Peng Lifa, or “Bridge Man,” as he has become known in allusion to Tank Man from the Tiananmen demonstrations in 1989, demanded elections and reforms. How have urban Chinese been able to be so content or even happy despite their lack of political freedom? The class readings will introduce you to different kinds of activists who have confronted the authoritarian state since the late 1990s, among them human rights lawyers, reporters, environmental activists, feminists, religious activists, and labor activists. We will ask whether freedom, an obviously Western notion, is useful as an analytical category to think about China. Does freedom translate across the West/non-West divide?

AS.310.339.description: This course explores the ways in which thematic and visual traditions are pictured, represented and conveyed across generations of filmmakers in landmark works of East Asian cinema. We will highlight the early films of Ozu and Kurosawa, engage with the legacies of Kim Ki-young and Im Kwon-taek, and study the works of Hou Hsiao-hsien and Wong Kar-wai in their aesthetic and political contexts. An orientating question for the course will be: What role do love and loyalty play in the stories that unfold on the screen? Students are not expected to have prior language background in Chinese, Japanese, or Korean.

AS.310.431.description: The East Asian Studies Senior Honors Thesis Seminar is a workshop for EAS majors writing an honors thesis. It is a year-long course with meetings scheduled in both the fall and spring semesters. Please note that in order to qualify for honors in the major, the thesis must receive a final grade of A- or better. Students will receive credit for the seminar regardless of whether their thesis qualifies for honors.

AS.310.432.description: This course is the continuation of Senior Thesis Course AS.360.431 for students completing their thesis in the East Asian Studies program.

AS.310.501.description: Students carry out an independent research project involving East Asia.

prereqs.text: You must request Customized Academic Learning using the Customized Academic Learning form found in Student Self-Service: Registration > Online Forms.

AS.360.105.description: Explore the University. Engage with people. Empower yourself. Chart your expedition at Hopkins. In this course for new and those returning from an LOA, students will explore Hopkins’ academic resources and opportunities to integrate their academic, career, and personal goals for college and beyond. Students will be exposed to topics including learning strategies, academic planning, and campus culture. Students will develop a personalized plan for success and make some new friends.

AS.360.106.description: Explore new opportunities. Strengthen your skills. Build your future. This course is designed for continuing Hopkins students who want to build academic momentum and make the most of their Hopkins experience. Through topics such as advanced learning strategies, academic planning, research and internship preparation, career exploration, and campus engagement, students will strengthen the knowledge, skills, and connections needed to thrive at Hopkins and beyond. Students will deepen their understanding of university resources while developing a personalized toolkit for academic success, career readiness, and personal growth.

AS.360.111.description: Death in the modern West is often a distant affair with the newly deceased being transported to far flung cemeteries or quickly cremated. Ancient mortuary practices often challenge modern norms by keeping the deceased close, corporally and spiritually. This course will introduce students to the archaeology of death and burial through the examination of the unique burial practice of intramural burials: burying deceased family members under the floors of houses. Case studies will be drawn from the Neolithic and Bronze Age Near East to clarify the transformational process of the newly deceased becoming an ancestor, and the social, legal, and spiritual consequences that process could incur. Students will consider these key questions: How are the stages of social transformation demonstrated through the bodily treatment of the deceased? How does the textual evidence support or contradict the interpretations of the archeological evidence?

AS.360.116.description: For students who desire to work in the health professions, it is imperative that they gain a well-rounded understanding of medicine. This course exposes students to the profound human experience of death and dying through hospice service and guided reflection. Students will explore the realities of illness, the limits of medicine, and the importance of prioritizing the comfort and dignity of those they support. Students will analyze the ethical challenges in end-of-life care, including how medical decisions intersect with social justice as well as cultural and religious beliefs. Through topics such as human suffering, compassion fatigue, grief, and wellness, students will reflect on the emotional demands of compassionate caregiving and apply appropriate communication strategies in hospice settings. Students will also critically reflect on the role of hospice in health care and be able to articulate what hospice offers to patients and caregivers.

AS.360.252.description: What is a good life? What does it take to live a good life? We will explore these and related questions in a learning community through engagement with several religious, philosophical, and intellectual traditions as they imagine living well, including Islam, Confucianism, Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism, Hinduism, Utilitarianism, and Postmodernism/Deconstruction. Across these traditions, we will consider both their distinctive approaches and the questions they share about meaning, purpose, responsibility, and human flourishing. The course will be shaped by reading and discussing ancient and contemporary wisdom texts, visits from individuals who understand their lives to be shaped by the traditions in question, and the adoption of an intentional practice over the course of the semester. In short, the course will ask students not only to study different visions of the good life, but also to consider what those visions might mean for how they choose to live.

AS.360.261.description:
Democratic political systems can go a very long time without making critical policy reforms, even when the policy gains from doing so are very large. Economists, for example, find that decades of inaction on reforming immigration policy are leaving “trillion dollar bills on the sidewalk.” How can we explain and shape the tendency of democratic systems, and the United States in particular, to forego large social and economic returns from policy change? Drawing on the literature on policy dynamics, polarization, gridlock and path dependence, this class will apply larger structural theories to the specific case of immigration reform, which despite multiple efforts has not seen major legislation in forty years. Students will also be asked to draw lessons from often surprising policy breakthroughs to develop specific recommendations for political strategy that will be presented to experienced participants in immigration policy.
Fridays in DC! Transportation and lunch provided.
*This course is part of a three-course Friday program at the Bloomberg Center in Washington, DC; students are encouraged to enroll in two of the three courses.*

AS.360.263.description:
AI systems are already capable of superhuman feats of reasoning, including solving mathematical problems that have stumped leading mathematicians for almost a century. They can code and use computers more effectively and much faster than the world's most talented programmers. They can work in swarms of thousands of agents, pursuing a common goal, and are becoming increasingly capable at AI research itself. We are on the cusp of building artificial general intelligence (AGI); by some understandings of that term, we are already there and on the path to superintelligence. Scenarios once dismissed as sci-fi, such as loss of control to rogue AI systems, are now within the technological horizon. We face an unprecedentedly risky technological transition and a period of social revolution whose precedents are soberingly grim. This raises two questions. First, can we stop what we've started and, if so, should we? Second, if we go forward, how do we steer a course that avoids the most egregious risks while preserving fundamental liberal democratic values? Success will require pulling every lever available, from technical interventions in AI systems, to regulations targeting AI development and deployment, to broader adaptation of our social institutions and the moral and political theories underpinning them. This course introduces AGI governance: the field concerned with either steering society safely to the AGI era or halting on its border. Students from all backgrounds are welcome but should have some familiarity with the technical basics of AI and frontier AI.
Fridays in DC! Transportation and lunch provided.
*This course is part of a three-course Friday program at the Bloomberg Center in Washington, DC; students are encouraged to enroll in two of the three courses.*

AS.360.264.description:
Americans today are confronted by the challenge of living, governing, and making policy together when our disagreements are more intense and more far-reaching than ever before. This interdisciplinary, seminar-style class will attend to various elements of our current moment, from the sometimes irrational and tribal aspects of human nature, to illiberalism and political polarization, gridlock, doubts about the efficacy of democracy or the benefits of pluralism, and loss of trust in institutions. Students will practice civil discourse and work to build trust and community across divides while discussing a variety of real-world political issues, including immigration, healthcare, AI regulations, affirmative action, guns, crime, and policing. The course’s Washington, DC location will bring the added benefits of special guest speakers, events, and sessions with SGP faculty with expertise in various fields.
Fridays in DC! Transportation and lunch provided.
*This course is part of a three-course Friday program at the Bloomberg Center in Washington, DC; students are encouraged to enroll in two of the three courses.*

Students who have taken AS.001.118,

AS.360.325.description: Citizenship, identity, and access are matters of media—the products of documentation, record-keeping, and the assignment of data to people and places. From passports and Social Security numbers to email addresses and digital profiles, individuals are made legible through media systems that identify, sort, and authorize. This course approaches digital citizenship and media literacy from a media-theoretical perspective. Drawing on cultural techniques research, media logistics, and German media theory, we examine how infrastructures of inscription, address, and circulation shape what it means to be a citizen in informational societies. Rather than treating “digital citizenship” as a matter of etiquette or “media literacy” as simply critical consumption, the course reframes them as problems of infrastructure, history, and technique.
restrictions: Hopkins Semester in DC Students Only

AS.360.393.description: Whether seen as ivied citadels of knowledge or ivory towers of privilege, universities can feel timeless to those who walk their halls. However, American higher education is the product of four centuries of change, over which ministerial schools evolved into billion-dollar institutions that concurrently sustain advanced research, residential communities of students, professional schools, and sports empires. This course covers the history of higher education in America from the colonial era to the present, addressing topics such as the purposes of colleges and universities, their relation to their cities, states, and nation, curriculum and pedagogy, access and inclusion, academic freedom, funding structures, and campus culture. It will survey a range of institutions, highlighting the multiplicity of higher education in the United States, but special focus will be given to the history of Johns Hopkins – the first American “research university.”

AS.360.394.description:
A long-standing barrier to substantive scholarship in the computational humanities is the technical implementation of experiments and methods. A powerful coding agent like Claude removes much of that friction and lets us focus on the core intellectual task of translating humanistic questions into experimental design, performing these experiments, and interpreting their results back into humanistic terms.
In this seminar course, participants will translate their historical and literary questions into falsifiable hypotheses and perform experiments that clarify and produce understanding about the phenomena involved. After orientation and planning over the first month, meetings will be devoted to presenting and discussing progress on each student's research project.
This course is intended to enroll a small number of advanced undergraduate and graduate students. Strong outcomes will hinge on participants starting from a baseline of simple computational (programming) experience, e.g., via JHU's Gateway Python or Harvard's CS50, and bringing tangible, specific humanistic questions to the table. An engaged, well-prepared student may reasonably hope to publish in a selective venue based on research performed in this course.

AS.360.395.description: This course is a semester-long investigation into how the conditions of humanistic inquiry – questions of who we are, how we live, and how we find meaning through reflecting on our experiences of the world – are sustained by nuts-and-bolts organizational work. This course is designed around a series of site-based seminars that integrate humanistic training and expertise with the practical realities of sustaining a public-facing cultural organization, with intervening weeks dedicated to scholarly reading about the relationship between place and intellectual life. Partner organizations will include museums, historic estates, and theater/performance companies. This course is anchored by a vision of the humanities that is as pragmatic as it is theoretical, assuming that today’s undergraduates are not just future practitioners, but also future administrators and patrons of public culture. In lieu of a final paper or exam, students will design and present their own organizational prospectus.

AS.360.415.description: The schism of professional philosophy into distinct discourses – analytic and continental philosophy – was a defining event in twentieth century intellectual history. Even in a discipline prone to stark division, the analytic-continental divide was an exceptional case, creating a gulf of acrimony and neglect across the discipline of philosophy. This course examines the rift between analytic and continental philosophers as both an intellectual and social phenomenon. Students will read works from both traditions, learning how members of each conceived of the methods, aims, and subject of philosophical inquiry. Against this backdrop, they will explore the history of disciplines, the consequences of methodological schism, and the possibility of communication between different conceptual paradigms. Because analytic and continental texts are rarely taught within a single course, this seminar provides a unique opportunity to consider what the domain of philosophical knowledge is and how such knowledge should be pursued.

AS.360.460.description: In this research seminar, students learn research methodologies while pursuing their own lines of inquiry. The course will be taught by faculty with active research agendas relevant to the semester’s theme. Students will work to address common research challenges and to strengthen their own and each other’s projects via discussion, thus enabling the cohort to have research method conversations and workshop drafts in a supportive group setting. Innovative and productive research requires intellectual community, and the seminar would provide it. Research projects, while tailored to students’ interests, will intersect in a meaningful way with the semester’s topic.
restrictions: Hopkins Semester in DC Students Only

AS.360.461.description: In this course, students learn from experts in the field as connected to the semester’s theme. The practitioners will present on their field of expertise thus providing students substantive engagement with a variety of perspectives relating to the central theme. Discussions with Hopkins Semester faculty will provide connection and framing for engagements with external stakeholders. Additional skills potential for development in this course include enacting policy in the world (networking, negotiations, public speaking, project management, (Political) Risk Analysis, Lobbying and Advocacy, Applying for Federal Jobs, Consulting), and others relevant to subsequent themes.
restrictions: Hopkins Semester in DC Students Only

AS.360.474.description: Historians have argued that Americans experienced a “thinning of society” during the second half of the twentieth century. Structures and metaphors that supported mutualistic organization, solidarity, and politics were vitiated or replaced by market-oriented institutions and political ideologies that gave primacy to individual liberty. To explore and explain these dynamics, this seminar will alternate between reading monographs in American intellectual history and texts from social theorists who challenged the limits of mainstream American political discourse, such as W.E.B. Du Bois, John Dewey, and Iris Marion Young.

AS.360.501.description: This course involves a specially designed project related to the student’s connection with the Hopkins Semester DC theme. On completion of this course, the student will be able to discuss how their work contributes to the advancement of the substantive theme explored in the semester. The student-designed project may be related to each student´s current employment context or developed in agencies or organizations that complement student’s research and experimental background.

AS.360.624.description: You do not need to register for any course in SIS. Within six weeks after course completion, the following entry will appear on your JHU transcript: “AS.360.624 – Responsible Conduct of Research (Online)"

AS.360.625.description:
Through a discussion-based curriculum, the Responsible Conduct of Research course introduces students to key research issues: academic ethics, animal subjects, conflict of interest, data management and authorship, and human subjects.
Attendance to all meetings is required to receive credit for the course. The add deadline is one week prior to the course start date. Instructor will send out the zoom link the 1st day of class or the day before.

A long-standing barrier to substantive scholarship in the computational humanities is the technical implementation of experiments and methods. A powerful coding agent like Claude removes much of that friction and lets us focus on the core intellectual task of translating humanistic questions into experimental design, performing these experiments, and interpreting their results back into humanistic terms.
